prompt.context: Penguins have evolved. Now they can talk and they are organized as an advanced society. The ambassador of Penguinland (former Antarctica) has reached out to Bain & Company because he is worried about the growing population growth of penguins. Currently, there are about 23 million penguins and the population is growing 32% per year.
prompt.question: How many penguins can live at Penguinland and what is the best way to accommodate everyone?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any predators in Penguinland?
clarifying_info.a: The penguins negotiated with all predators. The polar bears now live in a Zoo in San Diego and the whales live at Sea World.

clarifying_info.q: Is there enough food for all the penguins?
clarifying_info.a: There is a lot of food all over the ocean. It is more than enough to feed every penguin.

clarifying_info.q: What are the living arrangements of the penguins?
clarifying_info.a: They are all married and have a baby penguin. They need space for both penguins to live and a nest for the baby. Penguins do not need space for leisure — they need space just to sleep.
Penguins must eat every day or they will die. Even if a penguin stays in the ocean for only 1 second, it is enough to eat one fish.

clarifying_info.q: What is the area of Penguinland (Antarctica)?
clarifying_info.a: See Exhibit 1 — a map of Penguinland. You may approximate the map to a square.

clarifying_info.q: How long is the shortest day in Penguinland?
clarifying_info.a: The longest day of the year has 22 hours of sunlight, so the shortest day has only 2 hours of sunlight. Penguins only walk and eat during the day; they must sleep the whole night.

clarifying_info.q: How fast can a penguin walk?
clarifying_info.a: The average penguin leg is 20 cm; the average human leg is 1 m. Humans walk at an average of 5 km per hour. Walking speed scales with leg length.

clarifying_info.q: How big is a penguin? How big is a nest?
clarifying_info.a: Penguin size = 1 m². Nest size = 1 m².

exhibits.title: Penguinland Map
exhibits.shows: A map of Penguinland (Antarctica) with a scale marker indicating 4,000 km across one dimension

framework: Determine the total land area of Penguinland (approximate Antarctica as a square)
Determine how far from the ocean penguins can live (based on walking speed and shortest day constraint)
Calculate the total habitable coastal strip area
Determine space required per penguin family (male + female + baby nest + roads)
Divide habitable area by space per family to get maximum penguin population
Compare to current population and growth rate to assess urgency
Recommend best layout to accommodate everyone

questions.prompt: What is the total area of Penguinland?
questions.guidance: Candidate should approximate the Antarctica map as a square with side 4,000 km and compute area.

questions.prompt: How far from the ocean can a penguin live?
questions.guidance: Candidate must realize walking speed scales with leg length (penguin leg = 1/5 of human leg → penguin speed = 1/5 of human speed = 1 km/h). On the shortest day (2 hours of sunlight), a penguin must walk to the sea AND back, leaving at most 1 hour of walking in one direction → maximum distance = 1 km from the ocean. Excellent candidates proactively use the shortest day (not the longest) as the binding constraint.

math.setup: Penguin speed = (penguin leg / human leg) × human speed; max distance = (available daylight / 2) × speed
steps: Penguin leg = 20 cm = 0.2 m; human leg = 1 m
Time available for one-way trip = 2 h / 2 = 1 hour
Max distance from ocean = 1 km/h × 1 h = 1 km

questions.prompt: What is the total habitable area?
questions.guidance: Habitable land is a 1 km coastal strip around the perimeter of the square continent. Approximate as 4 rectangles of 1 km × 4,000 km (corners shared, exact answer is 15,996 km² but rounding to 16,000 km² is acceptable). Convert to m² for the next step.

math.setup: Habitable area ≈ perimeter × depth = 4 × 4,000 km × 1 km; then convert to m²

questions.prompt: How many penguin families can fit in the habitable area?
questions.guidance: Each family (1 male + 1 female + 1 baby) occupies a 5 m² block: 1 m² male, 1 m² female, 1 m² nest/baby, and 2 m² for two roads (penguins need roads to walk to and from the sea without collisions). Optimal layout: male and female side by side (2 m wide), nest behind or between them (1 m²), with Road 1 and Road 2 running parallel at 1 m each. Total footprint = 5 m² per family of 3 penguins.

math.setup: Number of families = habitable area / area per family; total penguins = families × 3
steps: Area per family = 5 m² (male 1 m² + female 1 m² + nest 1 m² + road 1 1 m² + road 2 1 m²)

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key drivers / dimensions to consider when determining how many penguins can live in Penguinland?

categories.name: Food & Survival
ideas: Access to ocean for daily fish
Shortest-day constraint determines max distance from sea
No food scarcity assumed in ocean

categories.name: Predators & Safety
ideas: Polar bears relocated to San Diego Zoo

categories.name: Space & Habitat
ideas: Each penguin needs 1 m² to sleep
Roads needed for two-way traffic to ocean
Coastal strip is the only habitable zone

categories.name: Mobility
ideas: Walking speed proportional to leg length
Must complete round-trip to ocean in shortest day (2 hours)

categories.name: Population Structure
ideas: Each unit = 1 married couple + 1 baby (family of 3)

categories.name: Geography
ideas: Antarctica approximated as a 4,000 km × 4,000 km square
Habitable zone = 1 km coastal strip all around

recommendation: Penguinland can support approximately 9.6 billion penguins at maximum capacity under the optimal coastal-strip layout (3 penguins per 5 m² in a 16,000 km² habitable coastal zone)
The current population of 23 million is well below capacity, but at 32% annual growth the population will exhaust coastal housing within roughly 15–18 years
The best accommodation strategy is to build a dense two-road grid layout along all four coastlines, allocating 5 m² per family of three
risks: Population growth rate may accelerate or coastal erosion may reduce habitable strip
Climate change could shorten Antarctic daylight windows, reducing the walkable distance
Ocean fish stocks could become a binding constraint if population approaches capacity
next_steps: Commission a detailed coastal survey to confirm usable strip width
Model population trajectory against capacity under 32% growth assumption
Establish a penguin urban-planning authority to allocate coastal plots systematically
